scenes.tts: On a July day in the Chesapeake Bay, a buoy at Stingray Point, Virginia, measured the air and the water. The air warmed by about eight degrees Celsius. The water just under the buoy changed by less than one and a half. Why does water behave so strangely, and how does that help keep living things alive?
scenes.visual: Two bars rise from a buoy: air tall, water short; a question mark over the water bar.

scenes.tts: A water molecule has one oxygen atom and two hydrogen atoms, joined by covalent bonds. A covalent bond is a bond where atoms share electrons. Oxygen pulls the shared electrons closer. So the oxygen end is slightly negative, and the hydrogen ends are slightly positive. A molecule like that is called polar.
scenes.visual: A bent labelled-block molecule: O and two H blocks with covalent bond bars; charges appear; the word polar.

scenes.tts: Opposite charges attract. The hydrogen of one molecule is drawn to the oxygen of a neighbor. This weak attraction between molecules is a hydrogen bond. In liquid water, hydrogen bonds form and break all the time. They are much weaker than the covalent bonds inside a molecule.
scenes.visual: Two molecules; a dashed bond links an H to the neighbor O; the dashes flicker; covalent bars solid.

scenes.tts: A solvent is a liquid that dissolves other substances. Water's charged ends pull salt apart. Cohesion is the attraction of water molecules to each other. At the surface it gives surface tension, which can hold up a water strider. Adhesion is the attraction of water to a different substance, such as paper.
scenes.visual: Three panels build in turn: salt crystal pulled apart; surface row of water blocks holding a strider; water climbing a paper fibre bar.

scenes.tts: Specific heat is the energy needed to warm one gram of a substance by one degree Celsius. For liquid water it is about four point one eight joules. For dry sand it is about zero point eight. Part of the energy added to water goes into stretching and breaking hydrogen bonds. So less of it shows up as a rise in temperature. One hundred grams of water that takes in eight hundred thirty-six point eight joules warms by two degrees. The same energy would warm dry sand by about ten.
scenes.visual: Energy split bar on hydrogen bonds; then two thermometer bars, water to 2, sand to about 10 for the same joules.

scenes.tts: Heat capacity is the same idea for a whole object. A big body of water, like the Bay, has an enormous heat capacity. So it changes temperature slowly. The fish, crabs, and grasses in it usually face gentler daily swings than the air over land does. Water is polar. Hydrogen bonds hold its molecules near each other. That helps explain why water warms slowly.
scenes.visual: Buoy bars return; chain of blocks: polar, hydrogen bonds, slow warming, steadier habitat.
